People of Fort Duffield

The story of Fort Duffield is the story of the men who built it, defended it, and endured one of the harshest winters of the Civil War atop the ridge above West Point. Their labor and sacrifice shaped the fort and the legacy it carries today.

William W. Duffield

The Fort’s Namesake

Colonel William Ward Duffield commanded the 9th Michigan Infantry, the regiment responsible for constructing Fort Duffield. His leadership during the early months of the war left a lasting impression on the men who served under him. The men, out of great respect for the Colonel, named the fort after his father Rev. George Duffield in his honor during its construction.

Learn About William Duffield →

Key Figures of the Civil War

Abraham Lincoln

Abraham Lincoln was a towering figure in American history—both literally and symbolically. Standing at 6’4”, he served as the 16th President of the United States from 1861 until his assassination in 1865. He is best known for leading the nation through the Civil War and abolishing slavery through the Emancipation Proclamation and the 13th Amendment.

Major General William “Bull” Nelson

William “Bull” Nelson was one of the most forceful and influential Union leaders connected to the early defense of Kentucky. Though he did not design or command Fort Duffield, his actions directly shaped the military conditions that made the fort necessary. His brief but important presence in West Point ties him firmly into the story of the fort, the Army of the Ohio, and the defense of Louisville.

Portrait — Major General William “Bull” Nelson

This portrait of Major General William “Bull” Nelson reflects the imposing presence and forceful leadership style that defined his brief but influential Civil War career. His actions in 1861–62 directly shaped the military conditions that led to the construction of Fort Duffield.

Panel 1 — The Man: William “Bull” Nelson

William “Bull” Nelson (1824–1862) was a towering naval officer turned Union general, personally selected by President Abraham Lincoln to secure Kentucky’s loyalty in 1861. Nelson organized Union Home Guards, armed loyal citizens, and prevented Confederate control of key regions.

By late 1861, Nelson commanded the 4th Division, Army of the Ohio. His presence in West Point came during the staging and preparation for the Tennessee campaign. Nelson’s career ended dramatically when he was shot and killed by Union Brig. Gen. Jefferson C. Davis at the Galt House Hotel in Louisville on September 29, 1862.

Panel 2 — Nelson’s Connection to Fort Duffield

Nelson’s work in 1861 directly shaped the environment that led to the construction of Fort Duffield. His recruitment of Union Home Guards created the manpower foundation for early defenses. His warnings about Confederate threats helped elevate Louisville’s strategic importance.

Nelson’s mission secured Kentucky. Fort Duffield secured Louisville.

Panel 3 — Where Nelson Operated in West Point

While Nelson did not maintain a formal headquarters in West Point, his division’s staging activities place him in several highly probable locations:

  • Ohio River Landing — embarkation point for the Tennessee campaign.
  • Camp Blair — winter encampment and organizational hub.
  • Supply depots near the river.
  • Road network toward Muldraugh Hill — the same routes Fort Duffield was built to protect.

Panel 4 — Unified Timeline

  • Summer–Fall 1861: Nelson organizes Union Home Guards across Kentucky.
  • November 1861: Fort Duffield is ordered and constructed.
  • Dec 1861 – Feb 1862: Buell establishes headquarters at West Point; Nelson’s division assembles nearby.
  • February 1862: Nelson’s division embarks from West Point for the Tennessee campaign.
  • September 29, 1862: Nelson is killed at the Galt House in Louisville.

General Don Carlos Buell

Major General Don Carlos Buell commanded the Department of the Ohio during the winter of 1861–62 and established his headquarters in West Point, Kentucky. The civilian home he used soon became known locally as General Buell’s Headquarters.

General William Tecumseh Sherman

General William Tecumseh Sherman was one of the most formidable and controversial figures of the American Civil War. Known for his relentless strategy and psychological warfare, Sherman reshaped military doctrine and left a legacy that still sparks debate today.

Colonel Charles Victor DeLand

Colonel Charles Victor DeLand was a distinguished Michigan officer whose Civil War service spanned multiple regiments and battlefronts. His legacy is tied to both the 9th Michigan Volunteer Infantry and the 1st Michigan Sharpshooters.

Robert H. Hendershot

Robert H. Hendershot became known as the “Drummer Boy of the Rappahannock" and is widely regarded as the youngest soldier to serve in the Civil War. His story begins with the 9th Michigan Infantry — the same regiment that built Fort Duffield.

As a boy in Jackson, Michigan, Hendershot spent his days around the soldiers’ camp, marching, beating on cans for drums, and mimicking the drills taught by the men of Captain Charles V. DeLand’s company.

On October 30, 1861, at just 10 years and 10 months old, Robert Hendershot was officially mustered into the U.S. Army at West Point, Kentucky — the youngest person ever mustered into the U.S. Military.

From Robert Hendershot, Youngest Civil War Hero by Monie Matthews.
Every trail, earthwork, and surviving feature of Fort Duffield reflects the lives of the men who served here. Their stories remain at the heart of the site’s preservation and interpretation.

item.title: William W. Duffield
item.dc:creator: fortduffield
item.content:encoded:
William Ward Duffield (1823–1907)

William Ward Duffield was a civil engineer, Mexican War veteran, Union colonel, military governor, railroad builder, coal executive, and later Superintendent of the U.S. Coast & Geodetic Survey. His life touched nearly every major sphere of 19th‑century American expansion — war, engineering, transportation, and federal science.

Early Life and Education

William Ward Duffield was born on November 19, 1823, in Carlisle, Pennsylvania, the son of Rev. George Duffield and Isabella Graham Bethune Duffield. In 1836, the family moved to Michigan, which he would consider home for most of his life. He later studied in New York and graduated from Columbia College in 1842 with a degree in civil engineering, earning a Master of Arts two years later. His early education placed him among the best‑trained engineers of his generation.

Mexican–American War Service

During the Mexican–American War, Duffield entered the U.S. Army as adjutant of the 2nd Tennessee Infantry and later served on the staff of General Gideon J. Pillow. After the war, he continued in the Army as a paymaster in California and became a founding member of the Society of California Pioneers. These experiences gave him deep military and frontier experience before the Civil War.

Engineering and Railroad Career

After leaving active military service, Duffield returned to civil engineering. He surveyed and engineered railroad lines in Michigan, Illinois, and New York, including work for the Detroit & Milwaukee Railroad and other early lines. His work demanded precision, discipline, and logistical skill — qualities that would later define his military command during the Civil War.

Civil War Command

Colonel of the 9th Michigan Infantry

At the outbreak of the Civil War, Duffield joined the Union Army and first served as lieutenant colonel of the 4th Michigan Infantry, seeing action at the First Battle of Bull Run. In September 1861, he resigned that position and accepted command as colonel of the 9th Michigan Infantry, a regiment composed largely of volunteers that quickly earned a reputation for order and readiness under his leadership.

In late 1861, Duffield and the 9th Michigan were dispatched to West Point, Kentucky. Their orders were to construct a defensive fortification to protect Union supply lines and secure the confluence of the Salt and Ohio Rivers. Working through bitter winter conditions, the regiment carved Fort Duffield into the hillside — a feat of endurance and engineering. Although Duffield did not personally design the fort, his leadership shaped the effort, and the fort was named in his honor.

Military Leadership and Wounds

In early 1862, Duffield’s abilities were recognized with broader responsibilities. He served on a military board of review in Kentucky, commanded the 23rd Brigade of the Army of the Ohio, and briefly acted as military governor of Kentucky. On July 13, 1862, while commanding Union forces at Murfreesboro, Tennessee, he was severely wounded and captured during a Confederate cavalry attack. His injuries prevented him from returning to field command, though he continued to serve in administrative and engineering roles supporting the Union war effort.

Life After the War

After the Civil War, Duffield resumed his work in engineering, mining, and railroads. He managed coal operations in several states and remained active in public service. In 1894, he was appointed Superintendent of the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey, one of the nation’s most important scientific and mapping agencies, serving until 1897. Throughout his postwar career, he remained closely connected to veterans’ affairs and public life.

Legacy

William Ward Duffield died on June 22, 1907, and is buried in Arlington National Cemetery. Fort Duffield remains the most visible legacy of his Civil War service. The earthworks his men built still stand above West Point, Kentucky — a testament to their labor, his leadership, and the enduring story of Union soldiers who shaped the landscape in defense of their country.

The Veterans Return: The 1895 Reunion at Fort Duffield

Thirty years after the winter of 1861–62, the soldiers who built and defended Fort Duffield returned to West Point. What followed was one of the largest veteran gatherings in the region’s history — a Grand Army of the Republic reunion that honored the men who lived, worked, suffered, and died on Muldraugh’s Hill.

Planning the Reunion

In 1895, Louisville prepared to host the 29th National Encampment of the Grand Army of the Republic (G.A.R.) — the national organization of Union veterans. West Point was invited to participate, and a local committee was formed under J. Lewis Williams and Frank R. Lord.

Using rosters of the regiments stationed at Fort Duffield — the 9th Michigan, 1st Wisconsin, 16th and 28th Kentucky, and the 1st and 18th Ohio — Lord sent personal invitations to every surviving soldier. The response was overwhelming. Thousands of middle‑aged veterans accepted.

One regiment, the 37th Indiana, was not invited. The reason is unknown — possibly lingering resentment toward Governor Oliver P. Morton, the strict discipline of Colonel Hazzard, or incidents involving Indiana troops during the war.

Original 1895 Reunion Letter (click to enlarge)

Provenance Note:
The original 1895 reunion letter and related materials are preserved in the author’s private collection.

A Sacred Return to Muldraugh’s Hill

Veterans described Fort Duffield as a “romantic spot” overlooking the Salt and Ohio Rivers. The earthworks and trenches remained intact, preserved much as they had been left at the close of the war.

Here the soldiers had:

  • Guarded the passes of the Muldraugh Hill range
  • Protected the Ohio River from Confederate invasion
  • Watched the turnpike toward Bowling Green and Nashville
  • Defended the pontoon bridge over Salt River
  • Slept, drilled, prayed, and mourned their dead

Many veterans returned to the cemetery where their comrades were buried beneath the trees. A poem quoted at the reunion captured the solemn mood:

“On fame’s eternal camping ground their silent tents are spread,
And glory guards with solemn sound the bivouac of the dead.”

How the Newspapers Described the Fort

Louisville newspapers covering the 1895 reunion were struck by how well Fort Duffield had survived the passage of time. Reporters noted that the earthworks and entrenchments still stood in remarkable condition, despite decades of weather and farming.

“Time and the elements and even the farmer’s plow have not brought any considerable change. The high walls of the entrenchments are overrun by verdure, but it requires only a small amount of imagination to see the cannon planted on the embrasures — to see blue‑clad men hurrying here and there — to hear the sharp orders of soldier life and see the white tents and flag of the country.”

The fort enclosed about five acres, with a sheer 150‑foot cliff forming the natural defense on one side. From the northwest point of the hill, the trenches followed a zigzag line in an irregular semicircle before reaching the cliff again roughly 200 yards away. Along this line were seven cannon positions.

The earthworks stood six to eight feet high on the inside, and from the top of the wall to the outside ground the drop ranged from 15 to 20 feet. The top of the wall was flat and wide enough for four men to patrol abreast.

Even after three decades, many traces of the wartime camp remained visible: stone chimneys, cook‑house excavations, the officers’ headquarters, and the path to the spring were all still recognizable to the veterans who returned.

A Community Celebration

West Point transformed itself for the reunion. Banners and flags lined the streets. The old wagon road up the hill was repaired. A Chautauqua‑style grounds was built at the fort, complete with a welcome arch, speaker’s stand, and even a private clubhouse.

Many of the old log cabins still stood — weathered, but recognizable. Piles of cannonballs remained near the abandoned gun emplacements.

Visitors were offered:

  • Guided tours of the fort
  • Historical talks by distinguished speakers
  • Exhibits of Civil War relics
  • A Kentucky dinner for 25 cents
  • Lodging for 25 cents a night

Excursions were arranged to both Fort Duffield and the birthplace of Abraham Lincoln.

Faces of the Reunion

Cpl. Charles Anderson, 9th Michigan Infantry — as a young infantryman garrisoned at Fort Duffield, and decades later at a regimental reunion.

“Old soldiers never die — they just fade away.” Left to right: George W. Green (Co. A), Sgt. Merrill Fuller (Co. A), and Sgt. William H. Ostrom (Co. K).

The 1895 Louisville Fireworks Disaster

The reunion coincided with Louisville’s hosting of the 29th National Encampment of the G.A.R. — the first encampment ever held below the Mason–Dixon line. More than 150,000 Union veterans and visitors flooded the city between September 4–15.

Scenes from the 1895 Fireworks Display

The Grandstand Collapse

Just before 8 PM, as the show was winding down, the eastern section of the grandstand built for the Citizen’s Committee collapsed. More than 4,000 people were on the stand at the time.

Thirty people were injured. Mrs. S. Hirschfield of 832 East Market suffered the worst injuries: a dislocated hip and a crushed right foot. Others sustained broken legs, sprained ankles, and dislocated shoulders. A panic was narrowly avoided.

The stand measured 45 by 150 feet and stood five feet off the ground. Had it been taller, fatalities would likely have occurred.

Provenance Note:
The invitation to the 1895 fireworks display and related reunion materials are part of the author’s private collection.

Legacy of the Reunion

The 1895 gathering cemented Fort Duffield’s reputation as one of the best‑preserved Civil War earthworks in the South. It also marked the beginning of organized preservation efforts — a tradition carried on today by the Sons of Union Veterans and the Fort Duffield Heritage Committee.

For the veterans who returned, the reunion was more than an event. It was a pilgrimage — a chance to stand once more on the ridge where they had endured hardship, forged friendships, and laid their comrades to rest.

First Skirmish at West Point

On September 9, 1861, West Point, Kentucky witnessed its first armed encounter of the Civil War. This brief but dramatic skirmish between Confederate cavalry and the Louisville Home Guard marked the moment when Union leadership realized the strategic importance of the ridge above town — the future site of Fort Duffield.

Louisville Home Guard & Confederate Cavalry Incident

September 9, 1861

As Union commanders scouted the confluence of the Salt and Ohio Rivers for a defensive position, General Robert Anderson dispatched Captain T. W. Gibson and a detachment of the Louisville Legion to West Point. Their mission: identify a site for a fortification that could protect Louisville and the vital river routes.

At daybreak, townspeople noticed a cloud of dust rising from the Louisville–Nashville Turnpike near present‑day 10th Street. A company of Confederate cavalry under Captain Mitchell Lapaille — a Louisvillian serving the Confederacy — rode into West Point. They were scouting the area for General Simon Bolivar Buckner and attempting to seize several store boats owned by Venne P. Armstrong. The boats, however, had already departed.

Unaware of the Confederate approach, Captain Gibson’s Home Guard had camped the night before at the point where the Salt and Ohio Rivers meet. They were in the process of ferrying across the river when the Confederate cavalry appeared. Half the unit was on each side of the river, leaving them dangerously split.

Gibson was eating breakfast at Young’s Inn — operated by Mrs. Ann Lewis — when the alarm sounded. A brief firefight erupted between the two forces. Neither side knew the strength of the other, and neither was eager for a full engagement. After exchanging shots, both units withdrew: the Confederates south toward Bloomington (now Fort Knox), and the Home Guard back across the river to Louisville.

Though small in scale, this skirmish was West Point’s first taste of war — and it accelerated the Union’s decision to fortify the ridge above town.

Bloomington (Fort Knox) and the Army of the Ohio

Bloomington, later known as New Stithton, stood on what is now Fort Knox. In late September 1862, General Don Carlos Buell’s Army of the Ohio took two and a half days to pass through the village. A reporter from the Cincinnati Daily Commercial described the scene:

“And now commenced the living stream that flowed incessantly by for two days and half… more than ten miles of soldiers on the march — infantry, artillery, and cavalry — filing past, regiment after regiment.”

Local farmer Milton Stith lost his cattle, sheep, and corn to the passing army. Although he received Quartermaster receipts, his postwar claims for compensation were denied. He is buried today in a Tarpley Cemetery on Fort Knox.

West Point’s Historic Homes

The city of West Point — lying directly beneath Fort Duffield — is rich in Civil War history. Several homes served as hospitals, officer dining rooms, and temporary headquarters during the winter of 1861–62.

Hospitals, Inns, and Officer Quarters

  • Private homes converted into makeshift hospitals for sick and wounded soldiers.
  • Young’s Inn, where Captain Gibson was eating when the skirmish began.
  • Homes used by Union officers for meals, meetings, and planning.

The James House Story

One of West Point’s most enduring local stories involves General Don Carlos Buell and the owner of the James House. During the war, Buell had a heated exchange with the proprietor. Years later, after the conflict had ended, Buell returned to West Point specifically to apologize for his wartime behavior — a rare gesture that left a lasting impression on the community.

Why This Skirmish Matters

  • It was the first armed encounter in West Point during the Civil War.
  • It revealed the vulnerability of the river crossing and supply routes.
  • It accelerated the Union’s decision to fortify the ridge — leading directly to the construction of Fort Duffield.
  • It highlights West Point’s role as a strategic crossroads long before the fort was built.

The skirmish, the movement of armies, and the stories of the town’s historic homes all form the essential backdrop to the creation of Fort Duffield. The ridge and the town are inseparable chapters of the same Civil War narrative.

item.dc:creator: fortduffield

West Point and the Civil War

Fort Duffield Park and Historic Site is a 175-acre resource in North Hardin County, Kentucky. Once part of the Fort Knox installation, the land was given to the City of West Point in 1978 through the National Park Service Lands to Parks Program for public recreation.

The historic site, Kentucky's largest and best-preserved Civil War earthen fortification, sits high atop historic Pearman Hill, 300 feet above the City of West Point. The fort is a Kentucky Landmark and part of the Civil War Discovery Trail.

West Point and Fort Duffield played an important role during the American Civil War in the last quarter of 1861 and throughout 1862. From this ridge above the Mouth of Salt River, the Union Army watched over rivers, roads, and supply routes vital to holding Kentucky in the Union.

Why West Point Mattered

Once neutrality in Kentucky was broken, the training and movement of troops for the Union Army began with great urgency. It was crucial that the Union maintain control of the rivers and roads in the area so that troops and supplies could be moved quickly and safely.

Supplies from Louisville were sent by steamboat on the Ohio River and offloaded onto wagons at West Point. The wagons then transported much-needed supplies to training camps and troops farther south.

Building Fort Duffield

Beginning in the fall of 1861, regiments from Indiana, Ohio, Wisconsin, and Michigan stopped at West Point on their way south. At first, troops were ferried across the Salt River from Jefferson County into Hardin County. Once Army engineers arrived, a pontoon bridge was installed.

The 9th Michigan Volunteer Infantry is credited with the construction of the fort. Before they left West Point, they also built a wooden bridge across the Salt River for supply and troop movements, which proved invaluable.

Sherman’s Strategy

General William Tecumseh Sherman ordered fortifications built at the Mouth of Salt River for several reasons. President Abraham Lincoln believed he must have Kentucky to save the Union, and Sherman understood that controlling this junction was essential.

Fort Duffield’s strategic location above the confluence of the Salt and Ohio Rivers allowed the Union to control both waterways. Since the railroad did not run through West Point at the time, Sherman recognized the importance of securing a land route for the movement of troops and supplies.

A fort at West Point ensured control of the rivers, kept land and water routes open for the Union Army, and helped protect Louisville from Confederate forces attempting to use those same routes.

Troops on the Move

In early 1862, brigades of Union troops were ordered to West Point to embark on steamboats down the Ohio River. Brigadier General William “Bull” Nelson, a Kentucky native, departed West Point with his 4th Division in February 1862.

In March 1862, the 9th Michigan left with the 23rd Brigade under the command of Colonel William W. Duffield. Thousands of soldiers passed through West Point on their way to the larger campaigns of the war.

After the War Moved South

After the Battle of Perryville in the fall of 1862, the main fighting moved farther south. The artillery and munitions at Fort Duffield were ordered returned to Louisville in December 1862, and the fort was left undisturbed except for occasional guerrilla raids.

This impregnable fortress, some 300 feet above the City of West Point, was never challenged in battle. However, its strategic position played an important role in the Civil War in Kentucky.

The 9th Michigan After Leaving West Point

Although the 9th Michigan Volunteer Infantry left West Point in March 1862 with the 23rd Brigade, their story continued far beyond Kentucky. After the Confederate withdrawal from the state, the regiment moved south with the Union Army into Tennessee.

By early 1863, the 9th Michigan was serving under Major General George H. Thomas in Murfreesboro, Tennessee, following the Battle of Stones River. The regiment acted as provost and headquarters guard, performed critical administrative duties, and helped stabilize the Army of the Cumberland during one of its most difficult reorganizations.

A remarkable firsthand account survives from this period: a detailed letter written on January 19, 1863 by Adjutant Anson A. Norton of the 9th Michigan to Lieutenant Colonel Hume. Norton describes the regiment’s condition, the aftermath of the battle, the challenges of rebuilding lost records, and the internal struggles among officers as the army prepared for the next campaign.

This letter offers a rare glimpse into the daily life, frustrations, and responsibilities of the officers who had once marched through West Point and built Fort Duffield. It shows how the regiment evolved after leaving Kentucky and how its men continued to serve the Union cause in the campaigns that followed.

Duffield Family History

A Union family whose service, sacrifice, and leadership helped shape the early defense of Kentucky.

The Duffield Family of Detroit

A Union family of faith, service, and sacrifice

The Duffields were one of Michigan’s most influential families during the Civil War. Led by Rev. George Duffield, a nationally known Presbyterian minister, the family became a symbol of Michigan’s early commitment to the Union. Multiple Duffield sons entered military service, carrying their father’s strong patriotic and religious convictions into the field.

Key Members of the Duffield Family

  • Rev. George Duffield (1794–1868)
    A prominent Detroit clergyman, abolitionist, and one of the most respected religious voices in Michigan. His sermons and writings inspired early enlistment and shaped public support for the Union cause.
  • Col. William Ward Duffield (1823–1907)
    Commander of the 9th Michigan Infantry and older brother of Henry. He led the regiment during its early campaigns and was wounded at the Battle of Murfreesboro.
  • Adjutant Henry Martyn Duffield (1842–1912)
    Twenty-year-old adjutant of the 9th Michigan Infantry. Later became a prominent Detroit attorney and served as a brigadier general during the Spanish–American War. A ceremonial sword presented to him on October 3, 1861 survives with a handwritten family dedication.

Why Fort Duffield Bears Their Name

When Union engineers selected the high ground above West Point, Kentucky for a new defensive earthwork in late 1861, the fort was named Fort Duffield in honor of Rev. George Duffield. His sons were among Michigan’s earliest volunteers, and the family’s influence symbolized the state’s devotion to the Union. The name reflected both the military service of William and Henry and the moral leadership of their father.

Original Sword Dedication — October 3, 1861

This is the original handwritten inscription presented to Adjutant Henry Martyn Duffield on October 3, 1861, shortly after his appointment to the 9th Michigan Infantry. The dedication accompanied a ceremonial sword given by a member of the Duffield family as the regiment prepared to leave Detroit for service in Kentucky.

Original inscription presented to Adjutant Henry M. Duffield, October 3, 1861.

Transcription of the Dedication

October 3, 1861

I give you this sword my dear boy to defend our beloved Government of the Union and the soldiers dear to my heart as it has always been.

I remember you bear not trifly hand — for

“Honor’s bright hilt is in your hand
For your flag undaunted stand
Heaven’s blessing upon it its stars show
With a lustre so pure and so warm
Like a beacon calm & safe bounty
but the safe way
They gleam thro the gathering storm
Like heart cheering light from afar
This all the task ’twixt they knew;
The same magic glow shall beam to inspire
And guide you to victory too”

I give this to my Country two bright gems, from the cluster of my Home.

Timeline: Henry M. Duffield, the 9th Michigan Infantry, and the Road to Fort Duffield

September 12, 1861 — Appointment as Adjutant

Henry Martyn Duffield is appointed Adjutant of the 9th Michigan Infantry. The regiment organizes at Fort Wayne in Detroit under the command of his older brother, Col. William Ward Duffield.

October 3, 1861 — Sword Presentation

A member of the Duffield family presents Henry with a ceremonial sword accompanied by a handwritten dedication blending patriotic duty and religious encouragement.

October–Early November 1861 — Training at Fort Wayne

The 9th Michigan continues drilling, equipping, and preparing for field service.

November 12–13, 1861 — Departure for Kentucky

The regiment leaves Detroit by rail and river transport, moving south into Kentucky.

Mid–November 1861 — Arrival at West Point, Kentucky

The 9th Michigan arrives at the strategic junction of the Ohio and Salt Rivers.

November–December 1861 — Construction of Fort Duffield

Soldiers of the 9th Michigan and 37th Indiana build the large earthen fortification overlooking West Point. The fort is named Fort Duffield in honor of Rev. George Duffield.

Research at Fort Duffield

Fort Duffield remains an active center of historical, archaeological, and cultural study. From subsurface mapping to archival discoveries, each project adds new insight into the fort’s construction, the soldiers who served here, and the deeper human history of the landscape they once defended.

Timeline of the Fort Duffield Region

  • Pre‑1600s: Shawnee, Cherokee, Chickasaw, Mosopelea, and Yuchi peoples travel, hunt, and compete for influence across the region that would become Kentucky.
  • 1600s–1700s: Indigenous cultures continue shaping the land through hunting, farming, trade routes, and seasonal movement.
  • Late 1700s: European settlers arrive; conflict increases as Native nations defend traditional homelands.
  • 1861: Union troops arrive in West Point, Kentucky, and begin constructing Fort Duffield.
  • Winter 1861–62: Soldiers endure harsh conditions; letters and accounts describe illness, hardship, and daily life on the ridge.
  • Modern Era: Archaeological surveys, GPR mapping, and archival research continue to reveal new details about the fort and the people connected to it.

Indian History of Kentucky

Long before the Civil War, the region surrounding Fort Duffield was shaped by the presence of several Native American nations. Shawnee groups moved from the north, while Cherokee and Chickasaw peoples traveled from the south of the Cumberland River. No single tribe held permanent control, and the area remained a shared and often contested homeland.

The tribes associated with Kentucky include the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Mosopelea, Shawnee, and Yuchi. Their way of life was influenced by the natural resources of the region — wooded hillsides, bluegrass plains, and fertile valleys. Many communities lived in Asi wattle‑and‑daub houses and practiced a mix of hunting, gathering, and small‑scale agriculture.

The name “Kentucky” is believed to come from the word “Kenta,” meaning “field” or “meadow.” Languages spoken by Native groups in the region were primarily Muskogean, and their cultural traditions aligned with the broader Southeastern Cultural Group.

For additional reading, visit:
History of Kentucky Indians – Warpaths2Peacepipes

Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR)

Letter 2 — December 3, 1861

Monroe D. Halladay, 9th Michigan Infantry

West Point, Kentucky

Original Letter

Transcription

December 3rd, 1861
West Point, Kentucky

Dear Brother,

I thought I would write you a few lines this evening. I feel a little more like writing to you than I have for some time. Your Brother,

Letter 3 — “Quick Letter” (Early 1862)

Monroe D. Halladay, 9th Michigan Infantry

West Point, Kentucky

Original Letter

Transcription

Early 1862
West Point, Kentucky

My Dear Brother,

We are about to start and we are in a hurry. The boat has already left the dock and we are waiting here for the Colonel. Mr. Simpson is going to leave, and I thought I would write you a few words to send by him. I think I shall send some money with him.

There is one who is sick. I told him her description, and if she could not go, I am. I wish I could go and see her. I am sorry to bring him home, as he thinks so greatly of him. He can tell you more of everything than I can write now.

Your Brother,
M. D. Halladay

This brief “quick letter” was written in haste as Monroe and the 9th Michigan Infantry were preparing to move from West Point, Kentucky. The boat had already left the dock, the Colonel was expected, and Monroe had only a moment to send a few lines home with Mr. Simpson. He planned to send money and mentioned a sick woman he wished he could visit, but could not. Letter 1 — November 29, 1861

Written by Lyman Halladay of the 9th Michigan Infantry, this is the earliest surviving Halladay letter from West Point, Kentucky. It captures the regiment’s first days on the ridge above town—cold weather, sickness spreading through the ranks, and the exhausting labor of building the early fortifications that would become Fort Duffield.

Original Letter Page

Download Letter 1 (PDF)

Transcription

West Point, Kentucky
November 29, 1861

Dear Parents,

I take this opportunity to write a few lines to let you know that I am well at present and hope these few lines will find you the same. We have moved our camp up on the hill opposite the town. It is a very high place and we can see a great distance up and down the river. We are building a fort here and it keeps us very busy. We have to cut timber and drag it up the hill, and it is very hard work.

The weather is quite cold here now and we have no tents yet, but we expect them soon. Some of the boys are sick, but not very bad. We have plenty to eat, such as it is, but it is not like home. I often think of home and wish I could step in and see you all, but that cannot be now.

We have not been paid off yet and do not know when we shall be. I want you to write as soon as you get this and let me know how you all get along. Give my respects to all inquiring friends.

This is all at present.
Your affectionate son,
Lyman Halladay

Interpretive Notes

  • Lyman describes the regiment’s move from the unhealthy river flats to the high ridge—an event confirmed in multiple DeLand letters.
  • His reference to “building a fort” is one of the earliest firsthand mentions of what would become Fort Duffield.
  • The lack of tents, cold weather, and sickness match the broader accounts of hardship during late November 1861.
  • His longing for home and uncertainty about pay reflect common themes in early-war volunteer regiments.

Pvt. John C. Love served with the Union forces stationed at Fort Duffield during the winter of 1861–62. His surviving letters offer a rare, personal look into the daily life, duties, and hardships experienced by the soldiers who built and defended the fort.

Note: These letters have been fully transcribed from surviving copies. The original handwritten pages have not yet been located. If the originals are found or donated in the future, they will be added to this collection.

Letter: November 1, 1861

Transcription

Transcribed from a surviving copy. Original manuscript not yet located.

West Point, Kentucky
November 1, 1861

Dear Parents,

It has been some time since I have written to you. I have had no time to write much. This afternoon it is raining for the first time since we have been here. The weather has been remarkably fine and warm since we have been in Kentucky.

We left Jeffersonville on the 21st for West Point, which is forty miles down the Ohio River. We embarked on board a large river boat such as I never saw before. It has two decks, and the water wheel is on the hind end of the boat. The boat left the landing at nine in the morning and went down the river at a rapid rate until we arrived at Louisville. Here we made a halt for the band to play. Leaving Louisville, we had to go through the ship canal, which is about four miles long.

Upon the Kentucky side it is generally level, but upon the Indiana side it is one of the wildest countries that I ever saw. The hills are almost like mountains, they are so steep and high. The sides of some of them are white with limestone.

We are encamped in an orchard that belongs to a man in the secession army. It is upon the bank of Salt River and about half a mile from the Ohio. There is one regiment from Indiana here, and Kellogg’s cavalry is on its way to join us.

General Buckner is within forty miles from us with fifty thousand troops, though we do not expect an attack. We have taken six spies and got them in the guard house. Forty of Company I’s men went down the river last night. They returned this morning bringing with them two secessionists, one of which has been in the rebel army.

The soil of Kentucky is clay. I have not seen sand enough since I arrived here to fill a pint cup. I have got pretty much over my cold, and I feel better than I did when I left Fort Wayne.

Anson is sick with the fever, though I think he will get along in a few days. Henry Redner is sick; the doctor says he has got the measles. He is pretty sick. Miron Wade has been sick, but he is getting quite smart again.

But I must close. I will write to you again as soon as I can.

From your only son,
John C. Love

P.S. Direct your letters to:
John C. Love
9th Michigan Infantry, Company C
West Point, Kentucky

Letter: November 7, 1861

Transcription

Transcribed from a surviving copy. Original manuscript not yet located.

West Point, Kentucky
November 7, 1861

Dear Parents,

It is with pleasure that I drop you a few lines to let you know that I am still alive and well, and hope these few lines will find you enjoying the same. I had hoped of receiving a letter from you ere this, or some of them that I have written to. But it takes some time to send a letter home and get an answer way down in this uncivilized country.

Kentucky and its inhabitants are fifty years behind the age. They are the most ignorant and inferior people that I ever saw so far as my observation has extended. Today it is as warm as it is in Michigan in September. We have had but one rainy day since we have been here.

There are two hundred men from our regiment and two hundred from the Indiana regiment to work upon Mistletoe Hill. They are throwing up breastworks and fortifying it as fast as possible, for General Buckner swears he will take dinner in Louisville in less than four weeks. He is down the river about forty miles from us, and he has but two ways to get to Louisville: one is up the river past us, and the other is on the south of us about sixty miles.

We have six cannon with us which will be placed upon the hill as soon as possible. Then we shall have a commanding range of the Ohio of four miles and all the roads this side of the hill.

Anson has been sick about a week but is a great deal better today. Henry Redner has been sick with the fever; he is not so well today, though I think he will get along after a little. There would be but few sick if we had good water to drink. We use river water to drink and for cooking.

Sam Graham is the cook for the company and is a good one. We have heard that Charleston and Fort Sumter have been taken, but do not know for certain whether it has or not.

I wish that you could send me the Tribune after you have done reading it. You can put a wrapper around it. It will cost you but a penny a paper, and it would do me a great deal of good.

I have heard since I commenced writing that we shall move across the river tomorrow or next day. I want you to write as soon as you receive this, and tell the folks to write to me if they think anything of me. They have more time to write than I have.

Goodbye for this time.
From your obedient son,
John C. Love

Direct your letters to:
John C. Love
Company C, 9th Michigan Infantry
West Point, Kentucky

Letter: November 20, 1861

Transcription

Transcribed from a surviving copy. Original manuscript not yet located.

West Point, Kentucky
November 20, 1861

Dear Parents,

It is with pleasure that I sit myself down after my day’s work is done to write you a few lines to let you know that I am well, and hope these few hasty lines will find you all enjoying the same blessings. The boys that went from there are all well except Henry Redner, and I think that he will get along after a little. Anson has had the toothache tonight very bad, but he has got so that he is able to work again.

There are five in this tent writing at present to their parents and friends, and it is so every night and every day that they are not at work. We moved from the place that we were when I wrote you last. We are camped now upon Muldrough’s Hill, just back of the fort.

We have all been at work digging the intrenchments. There were two hundred men of the First Wisconsin Regiment at work with us, but they will soon leave us to go to Elizabethtown. There have been six regiments passed this point within the last two weeks for the same place.

The report is quite current here that General Buckner has been surrounded, though we cannot tell anything about the reports that are circulated here.

I received a paper from you or Sam, and I do not know which, but it was thankfully received whoever sent it. Tell Sam that I will write to him as soon as I get time. Tell the folks around there that I like soldiering much better than I expected, and stand it first rate yet.

The weather is quite warm and pleasant here. I sent you a map of our encampment to show the position that we were in. When you write, I want you to let me know whether you received it or not, and write about the weather.

I received a letter from Aunt Harriet and will send it in this letter. I wrote to her yesterday. Father, I think you had better keep Frank to work for you as long as you can.

But I must close, for the drums are beating for roll call. Write as soon as you receive this, and tell the folks to write.

Yours truly,
John C. Love

P.S. Direct to:
John C. Love
Company C, 9th Michigan Infantry
West Point, Kentucky

Letter: December 1, 1861

Transcription

Transcribed from a surviving copy. Original manuscript not yet located.

West Point, Kentucky
December 1, 1861

Dear Father and Mother,

I received a letter from you Friday and was glad to hear from home once more, and to hear that you were all well. I was very glad of the postage stamps that you sent me, for I was out and could not get them here very well. I enjoy pretty good health and feel first rate. The boys are all feeling good except those that are in the hospital.

There are not quite as many sick as there were two weeks ago. They are getting over the measles, and when they are well there will be but little sickness. Henry Redner was taken to the hospital yesterday. He has been sick about five weeks and is pretty hard up, though I think he will get along now after a little.

He is a first-rate boy, but is one that can never be a good soldier for this reason: he is one that is never contented and is always homesick.

The weather here has been very nasty and rainy for the last ten days. A week ago last Friday morning it commenced raining, and at noon it commenced blowing and blowed a perfect gale. It tore our tent down twice so that we had to take everything that we had out until we could sew and tie it up again.

Friday night it commenced snowing and it snowed about an inch deep, and yesterday before night it was all gone. Today it is quite warm and would be very pleasant if it wasn’t so muddy.

Yesterday there was a grand review of the regiment, but as there was nothing of any importance happened I will not dwell upon the subject. Here I am interrupted by the call for dress parade. The parade ground is upon a hill about a quarter of a mile west of us.

Major Hopkins of the Fusileers Regiment came into our camp about eight o’clock last night and stayed with Captain DeLand until two this afternoon when he returned to Louisville. He came here to receive orders from General Buell, who makes his headquarters at Louisville.

There is some talk that we shall move in a week or two, but I think we shall stay here some time, though I should like to go about two hundred miles farther south. If we stay here this winter we shall build some log houses to quarter in.

There are about fifty acres of timber slashed down and about fifty acres more to cut. We have good water, but it is a great deal of trouble to get it up the hill. The water comes from springs in a deep ravine to the south of us.

A word about our arms. The first that we had were old Belgian muskets. They were examined and condemned. Then we got some new guns of the same kind, and they prove to be a very poor gun. In a day or two we receive the musket.

We made a fireplace in our tent today. But we sleep warm every night since we received our new blankets.

Anson and Horace have written some to you and send it with this. I will send you some verses that an old woman got up that bakes cornbread for the soldiers.

But I must close this letter.

Yours truly,
From an honest boy,
John C. Love

P.S. Write soon and let me know if you got the money that I sent to Cooper and Thompson’s Bank. Tell the folks to write and give my love to all enquiring friends.

I did draw the map that I sent you.
J. C. Love

Letter: December 20, 1861

Transcription

Transcribed from a surviving copy. Original manuscript not yet located.

West Point, Kentucky
December 20, 1861

Dear Father and Mother,

I received a letter and three papers today from you, and was glad to hear that you were all well. I got a letter from Chauncy M. Crego Wednesday and he wrote that Mother’s health wasn’t very good this winter.

I haven’t been very well for the last week. I took a heavy cold last Saturday and it settled all over me so that I was so lame it was hard work for me to get around. So Tuesday I commenced taking the medicine which I got from Doctor Jones, and it has helped me so that today I feel quite like myself again.

I suppose what makes me some lamer than I should be is that last week I was vaccinated and it has begun to work. It was reported here that they were having the smallpox in Louisville and the Colonel ordered every man in the regiment to be vaccinated.

Anson and Horace are both well and enjoy themselves first rate. They both send their best respects to you all.

Thaddeus Vining has been sick with the fever three or four days, but I think he is better today. Anson Lewis has been sick in the hospital about a week with the fever, but this morning I hear that he is some better. Levant Bangs is at the hospital yet. I haven’t seen him in some time, though I heard the other day that his foot was gaining slowly.

The doctors of this regiment are such that I shouldn’t like to have doctor me. They give one kind of medicine for every disease. The medicines most commonly in use are quinine, ipecac, and opium, and sometimes calomel.

We are upon Muldrough’s Hill yet and expect to stay here this winter unless our men are repulsed at Bowling Green. It is reported here that General Buell sent word to Buckner that he must have all the women and children removed from town within twenty-four hours or surrender. Buckner sent back word that he would do neither and said that he was ready for company of any kind.

The report says that Buell took command in person Thursday, and there is a rumor this afternoon that Buell has whipped him out, though one cannot tell anything about flying reports nowadays.

I do not anticipate ever being in a battle. It does not seem any more like a rebel state where we are than it did when we were in Michigan. I wish that this regiment could move down where the main army were stationed so that if there was any fighting to be done we might have a hand in.

The fort is nearly completed. They have all of the guns mounted, seven in number, six smooth bore and one rifled cannon. They are savage looking things, I tell you, and when one is fired when you are in the fort it will almost raise him off his feet. Ten thousand rebels would have no business with us here.

Bowling Green is about ninety-five miles from here to the southwest of us. I received a letter from Frank Randall day before yesterday. He was at Elizabethtown and was in camp there with six other regiments. He said that he had not been able to get a pass and didn’t know whether he could come where I was or not.

I wrote to him yesterday and told him if he couldn’t come where I was to send those things which he brought for me on the stage to West Point. He wrote that he was well and liked the place very much. He cooks for his father and one of the lieutenants, so he has a pretty easy place.

The DeLand Letters (9th Michigan Infantry)

Captain Charles V. DeLand of the 9th Michigan Infantry left behind some of the most detailed and vivid firsthand accounts of the regiment’s early service at West Point, Kentucky. His letters, published in Jackson newspapers in late 1861, document the miserable first camp on the river flats, the rapid spread of sickness, the construction of the earthwork fort that would become Fort Duffield, and the daily challenges of guarding one of the key approaches to Louisville.

Indian History of Kentucky

Long before the Civil War, the region surrounding Fort Duffield was shaped by the presence of several Native American nations. Shawnee groups moved from the north, while Cherokee and Chickasaw peoples traveled from the south of the Cumberland River. No single tribe held permanent control, and the area remained a shared and often contested homeland.

The tribes associated with Kentucky include the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Mosopelea, Shawnee, and Yuchi. Their way of life was influenced by the natural resources of the region — wooded hillsides, bluegrass plains, and fertile valleys. Many communities lived in Asi wattle‑and‑daub houses and practiced a mix of hunting, gathering, and small‑scale agriculture.

The name “Kentucky” is believed to come from the word “Kenta,” meaning “field” or “meadow.” Languages spoken by Native groups in the region were primarily Muskogean, and their cultural traditions aligned with the broader Southeastern Cultural Group.

Capt. Charles V. DeLand, 9th Michigan Infantry

Published in the Jackson Citizen, Jackson, Michigan

Written from Camp Headquarters, 9th Michigan Infantry, West Point, Kentucky

Transcription

Camp Headquarters 9th Michigan Infantry
West Point, Hardin Co., Kentucky
Tuesday, November 12th, 1861

Editor Citizen,

Thinking a few lines and items from the 9th may interest you, I will fulfill my promise to “write occasionally.” As you already know, our regiment received orders immediately after arriving at Jeffersonville to march to this point. We found our first camp one of the most unpleasant, malarious, muddy, and intensely secession points in all Kentucky...

Respectfully,
C. V. DeLand

Research at Fort Duffield

Fort Duffield remains an active center of historical, archaeological, and cultural study. From subsurface mapping to archival discoveries, each project adds new insight into the fort’s construction, the soldiers who served here, and the deeper human history of the landscape they once defended.

Timeline of the Fort Duffield Region

  • Pre‑1600s: Shawnee, Cherokee, Chickasaw, Mosopelea, and Yuchi peoples travel, hunt, and compete for influence across the region that would become Kentucky.
  • 1600s–1700s: Indigenous cultures continue shaping the land through hunting, farming, trade routes, and seasonal movement.
  • Late 1700s: European settlers arrive; conflict increases as Native nations defend traditional homelands.
  • 1861: Union troops arrive in West Point, Kentucky, and begin constructing Fort Duffield.
  • Winter 1861–62: Soldiers endure harsh conditions; letters and accounts describe illness, hardship, and daily life on the ridge.
  • Modern Era: Archaeological surveys, GPR mapping, and archival research continue to reveal new details about the fort and the people connected to it.

Indian History of Kentucky

Long before the Civil War, the region surrounding Fort Duffield was shaped by the presence of several Native American nations. Shawnee groups moved from the north, while Cherokee and Chickasaw peoples traveled from the south of the Cumberland River. No single tribe held permanent control, and the area remained a shared and often contested homeland.

The tribes associated with Kentucky include the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Mosopelea, Shawnee, and Yuchi. Their way of life was influenced by the natural resources of the region — wooded hillsides, bluegrass plains, and fertile valleys. Many communities lived in Asi wattle‑and‑daub houses and practiced a mix of hunting, gathering, and small‑scale agriculture.

The name “Kentucky” is believed to come from the word “Kenta,” meaning “field” or “meadow.” Languages spoken by Native groups in the region were primarily Muskogean, and their cultural traditions aligned with the broader Southeastern Cultural Group.

Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR)

Ground‑penetrating radar surveys at Fort Duffield have revealed buried features, structural remains, and areas of historical activity across the ridge. These findings guide preservation decisions and deepen our understanding of how the fort was built, used, and experienced by the soldiers stationed here.

January 19, 1863 – Murfreesboro Letter
9th Michigan Infantry

This letter, written on January 19, 1863 from Murfreesboro, Tennessee, offers a rare firsthand look at the 9th Michigan Infantry in the aftermath of the Battle of Stones River. Adjutant Anson A. Norton wrote to Lieutenant Colonel Hume, describing the regiment’s condition, administrative burdens, and internal tensions as the army reorganized.

The 9th Michigan had passed through West Point, Kentucky in 1861–62, helping build Fort Duffield before moving south with the Union Army. This letter continues their story and connects the builders of Fort Duffield to the larger campaigns of the Western Theater.

Full Transcription — Letter to Hume, January 19, 1863

Murfreesboro, Tenn
January 19th, 1863

My dear Hume,

I had intended writing you long before this but I have been very busy indeed which, added to the fact that our rivals, like the Indian epistles of the white man’s mighty civilization, has reduced our time for not to hazard a letter that might not reach you.

When we first returned to the regiment we found it in very poor condition. Clothing being mis accounted to issue for more than this company, and I suppose also that a rein battalion with no proper officer present found we had not what they required and allowed the boys to get out of almost all articles of clothing and camp equipage. So I found work immediately to procure grounds for the Major, who is a most worthy officer, and said that I knew how to circumvent red tape officials better than the rest of them and made me a sort of temporary quartermaster.

During this week that we lay on the Franklin Turnpike and being miles from Nashville, I fitted the boys out with socks, stockings & I demand issued 500 prs of socks so you can see how they were equipped in that respect — harness and rubber blankets. All of which was a very simple matter, but having to dance attendance on the officers to get a requisition approved and mailed and however more to procure an order directing the issues took considerable time, and had it not been that I had a personal acquaintance with many of them and that the matter was a forgone to me, I doubt if I would have got them yet. You know how generously attentive to business and the benefit of the service some of our staff officers are.

A most lovely business what I invented when we joined there. The advance of the army here, reaching here the morning of Monday the 5th ? and entering the city among the first regiments.

Since then I have been very busy getting up the regimental papers and books which had not only been lost at the depot in July last but had also never been properly kept since I left the regiment in March last; and I found letters from Genl Robertson of Michigan and Genl Hume at Washington stating that no new returns for this regiment had been received since March 1862, & it has kept me hard at work and in addition thereto I have been appointed by Genl Thomas as Inspector Genl which adds to my duties considerably.

The regiment did good service here during the fight although not making any charge — this by checking a force which would otherwise have passed through the entire right wing of our army; and for this behavior were highly complimented by Genl Thomas Chief of Staff and by the General himself.

There is no reason that I can see why we should not now do well if the officers would do their duty. But I am sorry to say that there is not the zeal manifested by them that the circumstances demand. Parkinson could be one of the most efficient commanding officers we could desire, indeed I think he will be anywhere but here, but the besetting sin seems to have taken hold of him again and not a night passes that finds him in camp. He and our acting Major Captain Remick are generally night and gone.

Col. Major Robertson, who thinks I am a model soldier and an oracle on military matters, seems in despair and says “Well Adjutant, you and I have got the regiment to run through — I guess they had better let us run it altogether.” This course necessarily produces great dissatisfaction among the subordinate officers, especially those who were with us in July last and saw the circumstances. Nor can I blame them, to tell the truth I cannot.

I cannot sleep easy until I have personally gone through commands of the guards and ascertained that they are at their posts. I may ask for Col. Bankhurst to act — this very hurt for Renudo; a married man and one who has hopes and is striving for promotion; it is the very worst cause to take. The officers have lost all respect for him, and he has shown himself terribly ignorant of his duties.

At the time of the Bankhurst rendezvous summing, the Colonel had to send me to the left of the line to form it into shape. He (Renudo) had thrown out no guides and things muddled up like sheep with no formation whatever, were in imminent danger of being cut only by the frightened frightened and clamoring other panic.

Another source of discontent is the promotions that have been and are being made in the regiment. When I returned to the regiment I was told there would be trouble on this account. Having returned long ago a captaincy, I was feeling that the only objection to my taking one was a hopeless partiality, if any objection existed, and being guilty. Added to the fact that there was much work to be done in the Adjutant office before the regiment were in running order, I declined the recommendation offered by Major Wilhemsen, who very kindly as stated in his letter to the Governor.

Lieut. S. Barrows (SS), & I, Anson being the present pilots for and deserving of promotion, have been commissioned as captains. Two juniors — Lieuts Virginia, Emily, Wright-Purdy & Barrows (Anson) — who are among the best officers we have.

Norris’s commission the Colonel has omitted and written relative thereto to the Governor, but Barrows brought this into being and is a picture the consequence you can readily imagine. It does not signify after sensitive months hard service to be cut out of his promotion, while a soldier misfit obtains, by a junior and a poor officer, and it has caused great discontent.

But to look at the bright side of the picture, the “I I I”1

Mrs. G.P Duffield. has gained great credit for her part in the recent advance upon and retreat at Murfreesboro. She is well known at Nashville as the regiment that checked the stampede and has negotiated herself into the favor of Genl Thomas, who rumor says is going to be commander here vice Rosecrans, who will go to the Potomac.

The men are in good health and spirits, needing their somewhat, but in excellent discipline. Thomas comes over to see us often and seems well so far as it goes — he himself personally selected a camp for us the other day. We were coming from Nashville this week. Genl Thomas offered me, in behalf of the General, a place on his staff, but I had better turn it down — appointment after eight minutes’ experience — and the Major was very kind to me to leave the 9th, so I accepted the duties of a Quarter Genl with his help, my place for the regiment, and claim some of the privileges of a Quarter Master were with for me. The & fancy that are the better & more to every can and keeps off the blues.

I am sorry to be enrolled as Corporal — Major Wilkins quite sick and they sent him over to May. The camp this morning the Doctor says his tonic turn he will be sick. Philip gave a letter to people for him to attend to him at the camp — has passed him down a great coat.

The old Army regiments are active but plenty of men and much illness. All your acquaintances are fast — all except Major Minor, who joined the rebel service and entirely is stripped of malcontents and everything else. You write not shown it more of politics to write felt at home or in action. I don't mind it. Well here we must turn like as soon as an opportunity occurs. He will recruit for five or six dollars a month in the country. George sends to find a place for him — my sympathy. Mr. Rice, the man who keeps Pete — General Ny writing to be a minister over in a field with the convenient and a sit with the sermon.

Footnotes

1. The phrase “I I I” is almost certainly a reference to the Third Battalion of the 9th Michigan Infantry, written in Roman numeral form. Officers frequently referred to battalions as “I,” “II,” and “III,” and in handwritten letters these often appear as separate strokes. The writer is making a dry, humorous pivot: after describing the regiment’s internal problems, he notes that the Third Battalion was the “bright side” — the most reliable and least troubled part of the regiment.

Walking & Driving Tour of Louisville’s Lost Civil War Forts

During 1864–65, Louisville constructed a 10½‑mile arc of eleven earthwork forts to protect the city from a feared Confederate attack. Although the forts have vanished beneath modern neighborhoods, their story remains written across the ridges, roads, and river bends of the city.

This tour follows the original defensive line from west to east. Each stop includes modern landmarks, what to look for today, and a brief interpretive summary.

Stop 1 — Fort Southworth (Paddy’s Run)

Modern Location: Near Paddy’s Run Pump Station, west of N 36th St
Best Access: Drive
What to Look For: Subtle rise above the floodplain; the Ohio River bend

Fort Southworth anchored the western end of Louisville’s defenses. Its guns could sweep the river bend and support Fort Clark to the east.

Stop 2 — Fort Clark (36th & Magnolia)

Modern Location: 36th St & Magnolia Ave
Best Access: Easy street parking
What to Look For: Gentle ridge running east–west; long sightline toward downtown

Fort Clark guarded one of the main southern roads into Louisville and supported both Fort Southworth and Fort Karnash.

Stop 3 — Fort Karnash (Wilson Ave, 26th–28th Streets)

Modern Location: Wilson Ave between 26th & 28th
Best Access: Drive or short walk
What to Look For: Slight elevation above surrounding blocks

Fort Karnash filled the gap between Clark and St. Clair Morton, forming the mid‑western arc of the line.

Stop 4 — Fort St. Clair Morton (16th & Hill Streets)

Modern Location: 16th St & Hill St
Best Access: Drive
What to Look For: High ground overlooking Dixie Highway

One of the most strategically placed forts, it commanded the old Salt River Turnpike — today’s Dixie Highway.

Stop 5 — Fort Philpot (Algonquin Pkwy & 7th Street Road)

Modern Location: Near Algonquin Pkwy & 7th Street
Best Access: Drive
What to Look For: Rise controlling the 7th Street corridor

Fort Philpot protected the southwestern approaches and supported the L&N Turnpike defenses.

Stop 6 — Fort McPherson (Preston Hwy Corridor)

Modern Location: Near Preston Hwy & Eastern Pkwy
Best Access: Drive
What to Look For: Broad elevated ground; long southern sightlines

The largest and most heavily armed fort in Louisville, McPherson mounted a 100‑pounder Parrott rifle with a five‑mile range.

Stop 7 — Fort Horton (Merriwether & Shelby Streets)

Modern Location: Merriwether Ave & Shelby St
Best Access: Walkable neighborhood
What to Look For: Slight rise along the Shelby Street corridor

Fort Horton guarded the southeastern roads into Louisville.

Stop 8 — Fort Hill (Castlewood Ave / St. Louis Cemetery Ridge)

Modern Location: Ridge between St. Louis Cemetery & Castlewood Ave
Best Access: Park near Barret Middle School
What to Look For: Prominent ridge overlooking the Highlands

Fort Hill commanded the high ground between the central and eastern sectors of the defensive line.

Stop 9 — Fort Engle (Arlington Ave & Spring Street)

Modern Location: Arlington Ave & Spring St
Best Access: Walkable; steep terrain
What to Look For: Dramatic drop toward Beargrass Creek; rail corridor below

Fort Engle worked with Fort Elstner to protect the northeastern approaches and the canal system.

Stop 10 — Fort Elstner (Bellaire, Emerald & Vernon Avenues)

Modern Location: Clifton hillside above Beargrass Creek
Best Access: Walkable neighborhood
What to Look For: High spur overlooking the creek bend

Manned by USCT regiments, Fort Elstner anchored the Beargrass Creek line and protected the canal.

Stop 11 — Fort Saunders (Cave Hill Cemetery)

Modern Location: Inside Cave Hill Cemetery, on the eastern ridge
Best Access: Walk or drive inside cemetery
What to Look For: High ground east of the lake; views toward the Highlands

Fort Saunders completed the defensive arc, guarding the eastern approaches to the city.

Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) Research

Ground‑penetrating radar (GPR) has played a key role in understanding the hidden landscape of Fort Duffield. These surveys allow archaeologists to investigate sensitive areas—such as the probable Civil War cemetery— without disturbing the ground.

Download the Full 2014 KAS Report (PDF)

Ground‑Penetrating Radar Study (2014)

In 2014, the Kentucky Archaeological Survey conducted a detailed ground‑penetrating radar (GPR) study at Fort Duffield to help answer one of the site’s most enduring questions: Where exactly was the Civil War cemetery located?

For decades, local tradition placed the cemetery on a small rise near the fort. No headstones survive, and written records are scarce. To investigate the area without disturbing the ground, archaeologists used GPR — a non‑invasive technology that sends radar waves into the soil and records reflections from buried features.

The survey identified several subsurface anomalies that may represent grave shafts. Soil cores taken from selected locations showed some disturbed soil layers, but not enough to confirm burials with certainty. Because no excavation was performed, the results remain cautious. Still, the pattern of anomalies strongly suggests that this area is the most likely location of the wartime cemetery.

Today, the site is preserved as a quiet memorial space. The study helps us better understand the fort’s history and honors the soldiers who served here during the difficult winter of 1861–62.

Source: Philip B. Mink II and Jay Stottman, “A Ground Penetrating Radar Survey of a Probable Cemetery Location at Fort Duffield, West Point, Hardin County, Kentucky,” Kentucky Archaeological Survey, August 2014.

What Is Ground‑Penetrating Radar (GPR)?

Ground‑penetrating radar (GPR) is a non‑invasive method that allows archaeologists to “see” beneath the surface without digging. A small antenna sends radar waves into the ground and records how those waves bounce back from buried objects, soil changes, or voids.

By collecting many closely spaced readings, archaeologists can create map‑like images of what lies below. Features such as possible grave shafts, foundations, or trenches may appear as distinct shapes or patterns in the data. Because no soil is disturbed, GPR is especially valuable in sensitive areas like cemeteries and historic sites.
